name: Sweden

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally
paths.note: Capital income tax of 30% on realised gains and on dividends, with credit for foreign withholding tax. No wealth tax and no inheritance or gift tax; the children take over the parents' cost basis, so latent gains are taxed only when they sell.

paths.name: Investment savings account (ISK)
paths.note: Listed shares inside an ISK pay no tax on gains, dividends or withdrawals; the account instead pays 30% of a deemed yield of 3.55% (2026), i.e. 1.065% of the capital base above SEK 300,000 per person. Foreign withholding tax is credited against that tax. The rate follows the government bond rate each year and the tax-free level is not indexed. Each spouse holds half in an own ISK. Holdings of 10% or more are not allowed, which does not bind a diversified portfolio.

paths.name: Family holding company (AB)
paths.note: A Swedish AB owned by the parents pays 20.6% on gains and dividends of listed portfolio shares (below 10% of the votes there is no participation exemption), with credit for foreign withholding tax. A dividend to the passive owners is taxed at 5/6 x 30% = 25% (non-qualified unlisted shares). The AB shares are in the estate at value; Sweden has no inheritance tax, so nothing is due at death. Running costs are not in the tax file.

checks.working: Top marginal case, no allowances. Foreign dividends 200,000 taxed as capital income at the flat 30% (Inkomstskattelagen 65 kap. 7 §; PwC, Individual income determination) = 60,000, less the 15% foreign withholding credited (Lag 1986:468 om avräkning av utländsk skatt; credit limited to the treaty rate, here 15% x 200,000 = 30,000) = 30,000. Realised gains on listed shares 150,000 x 30% = 45,000. No wealth tax (abolished 1 January 2007, PwC Other taxes). Total 30,000 + 45,000 = 75,000.

Gains and dividends inside an ISK are not taxed; the account is taxed on a deemed income (schablonintäkt) of the capital base x (government bond rate on 30 November 2025, 2.55%, + 1 point) = 3.55%, minus the tax-free level of SEK 300,000 x 3.55% per person (Skatteverket, ISK page), taxed at 30%. The couple holds SEK 5,000,000 in each of two ISKs: (5,000,000 - 300,000) x 3.55% x 30% = 4,700,000 x 1.065% = 50,055 per account, 100,110 in total. Foreign withholding of 15% x 200,000 = 30,000 is credited automatically against this tax (Skatteverket, automatic foreign tax credit): per account the deemed foreign income 15,000/0.15 = 100,000 is below the account's schablonintäkt (5,000,000 x 3.55% - 10,650 = 166,850) and the credit 15,000 is below the Swedish tax 50,055. Tax 100,110 - 30,000 = 70,110.

The AB pays corporate tax of 20.6% (PwC, Taxes on corporate income) on portfolio dividends and gains: listed shares below 10% of the votes are not business-related, so there is no participation exemption (PwC, Corporate income determination). Dividends 200,000 x 20.6% = 41,200, less the foreign withholding credited up to the Swedish tax on that income (15% x 200,000 = 30,000 < 41,200; PwC, Tax credits and incentives) = 11,200. Gains 150,000 x 20.6% = 30,900. Total 42,100. No wealth tax. The AB's running costs are not in the tax file (no figure was found) and the 25% payout tax is excluded.

Sweden has no inheritance, estate or gift tax (abolished 2005; PwC: 'There are no inheritance, estate, or gift taxes in Sweden'). Estate of SEK 100,000,000 passing to three children: tax 0. The children take over the parents' cost basis, so the 30% tax on latent gains falls when they sell.
The AB shares are inherited like any asset and Sweden has no inheritance or gift tax (PwC, Other taxes): tax 0 on SEK 100,000,000 passing to three children.

assumptions: Top marginal case: about EUR 600k of dividends a year, so no personal allowances matter. The checks use 200,000 of foreign dividends and 150,000 of gains at 15% foreign withholding.
The couple split the portfolio evenly between two ISKs, one each, and so get two SEK 300,000 tax-free levels (the tax file now holds SEK 600,000).
The portfolio is assumed to enter the ISK or the AB without Swedish tax on its latent gains (for example funded with cash before arrival).
Shares of a passive family AB are assumed non-qualified (no owner active in the company), so a dividend is taxed at 25% and not under the 3:12 rules.
The ISK rate (1.065%) is the 2026 rate and moves with the government bond rate each year; the projection holds it constant.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: moving an existing directly held portfolio into an ISK or an AB is a sale at market value (Skatteverket, ISK page), taxed at 30% on the latent gain; the projection starts the structure with the full EUR 30M and has no one-off entry tax.
The AB's running costs (accounting, audit) are not in the tax file, so the AB checks carry none.
Whether the 5/6 reduction applies to every dividend from a passive family AB: Skatteverket's 'Om aktier' says there are cases without it. The statute chapter was not opened.
Inkomstskattelagen article numbers 65 kap. 7 § (30% rate) and 57 kap. 4 § (qualified shares) were not opened on a statute page.
Check the 2027 ISK rate when the 30 November 2026 bond rate is published, and the effect of the post-election government on ISK and 3:12.
